GDPR comes from the DPA in your contract

Regulations reach Claude through different mechanisms, and GDPR's is a contract. Anthropic's Data Processing Addendum (DPA), which includes Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), is built into the Commercial Terms of Service. An organization that accepts those terms has also accepted the DPA. You do not sign anything else or enable a feature. HIPAA works differently: there, an admin has to accept a BAA on a card in the Console. Anthropic's privacy policy, the DPA and its help articles describe how Anthropic handles personal data when it acts as a processor for its customers.

The contract follows the access path. The DPA described here covers commercial products such as the Claude API and Claude for Work, and consumer plans have their own terms. If you reach Claude through a third-party platform or service provider, that platform's terms of service govern your use. A GDPR review of a Bedrock deployment therefore starts with the AWS agreement, not with Anthropic's DPA.
The DPA sets up the processor relationship. Where inference runs and where data is stored are separate questions that you answer with configuration.
Checkpoint 1 of 6
Check yourself
An EU company calls Claude through Amazon Bedrock and processes customers' personal data. Their compliance team starts a GDPR review of this deployment. Which agreement should the review start from?

Data residency: inference geo and workspace geo
Two independent settings decide where Claude handles your data.
Inference geo
decides where model inference runs, and you set it per request or as a workspace default.
Workspace geo

decides where data is stored at rest and where endpoint processing, such as image transcoding and code execution, takes place. Only "us" and "global" exist as inference geos, and "us" is the only workspace geo available.
Pinning one request to US inference and reading back where it actually ran
python
The default is "global", which lets inference run in any available geography. Each response's

field records where inference actually ran, so you can log it as evidence. The parameter works on Claude 4.6 and later models. Sending it to Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5 or anything older returns a 400 error. In the Batch API, each request can set its own value.
Predict first
A workspace has allowed_inference_geos set to ["us"]. A developer's request sets inference_geo to "global". What happens?
The API returns an error
The request runs globally, because a per-request value always overrides the workspace
The API quietly runs the request in the US instead
Workspace settings are how you turn a residency rule into something enforced.
rejects any geo not on the list.
fills in when a request leaves the parameter out. You set both through the Console or under the Admin API's

field, and they apply to every key in the workspace, so one developer's missing parameter cannot send traffic outside the allowed geos. Organizations that had opted out of global routing under the old setting were migrated automatically to
for both settings.

Workspace geo is permanent. You choose it when you create the workspace, in the Workspace geo field on the Create workspace page, and you cannot change it afterwards. If the storage location is wrong, the fix is a new workspace. US-only inference costs 1.1x the standard rate on Claude 4.6 and later models. Rate limits are shared across all geos, so pinning to "us" does not give you extra capacity.

FedRAMP: authorize the environment, not the model

FedRAMP and DoD Impact Levels certify cloud services, not models. A Claude model is a software component that runs inside an authorized environment, and the customer's compliance posture comes from that hosting platform. "Is Claude FedRAMP High?" is therefore the wrong question. The right one is which environment you run Claude in and what that environment is authorized for.

Three FedRAMP High paths exist. Claude for Government is Anthropic's own FedRAMP High authorized application, with Anthropic as the contracting and billing party. Claude through Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) is approved for FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5 workloads. Claude through Google Vertex with Assured Workloads is also FedRAMP High. Bedrock goes further: Claude is available in the AWS Secret region (IL6), and ITAR data can only be processed in Claude through Bedrock.

For an agency already inside a GovCloud authorization boundary, Bedrock in GovCloud is the direct fit. It runs on AWS-controlled infrastructure the agency already has, and AWS is the data processor. The Claude Platform on AWS documentation itself sends FedRAMP High and IL4/IL5 workloads to Bedrock. The standard Claude API is not on the list of FedRAMP-authorized paths. Neither is Claude Enterprise bought through AWS Marketplace, which is not FedRAMP authorized. Consumer plans are not a government path at all.

Retention records a compliance reviewer will ask for
Audits usually come down to two questions: what records exist, and for how long. The events themselves and how they reach your systems are covered in
Audit events and their routing
. The retention periods are separate from both ZDR and HIPAA readiness, and a reviewer will check them one by one:
Activity Feed:
6 years.
claude.ai chat, file and project content:
follows the organization's policy in Organization settings > Data and privacy, unless a user deletes it sooner.
Local session transcripts (Claude Code, Cowork):
6 years by default, or the organization's custom retention period when a finite one is set.
Remote Cowork session transcripts:
6 years unless a user deletes the session.
Compliance API:
does not capture local sessions that run under ZDR. In HIPAA-ready organizations, it captures only Claude Code and Cowork local sessions and keeps those transcripts for 30 days.
Copies on developer machines need their own answer.

in managed settings makes every computer delete old session data after the same number of days, which you set to match your records policy. In Claude for Government, a hash-chained audit log records every administrative action, and administrators can review it directly in the product.

The local session transcripts, kept for 6 years like other session transcripts

Practise it for real
Pin a workspace's inference to the US, then confirm from API responses that requests are enforced and actually run there.
In the Console, set the workspace's allowed_inference_geos to ["us"] and default_inference_geo to "us".
Why:
Workspace settings enforce the policy for every key, so you are not relying on each request to set it.
You should see:
The workspace's data residency settings show "us" as the only allowed geo.
Send a Messages request on a Claude 4.6 or later model with inference_geo="us" and print response.usage.inference_geo.
Why:
The usage field records where inference actually ran, and you can log it as evidence.
You should see:
The printed value is "us".
Send the same request with inference_geo="global".
Why:
This checks that the allowlist blocks traffic a developer tries to send elsewhere.
You should see:
The API returns an error instead of running the request.
Send a request with no inference_geo parameter.
Why:
This checks that the workspace default fills in when a request leaves the parameter out.
You should see:
response.usage.inference_geo reads "us".
